content:
Quick answer: Water-based exercise can make movement more comfortable for some people with arthritis. For hip or knee osteoarthritis, research suggests small, short-term improvements in pain and function. Swimming lengths, an exercise class and physiotherapist-led hydrotherapy are different activities. Choose an approach that fits your health, ability and confidence, with advice when needed.

What NICE recommends

NICE NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the person with osteoarthritis. It does not prescribe one swimming stroke, pool temperature or session length for everyone. Some discomfort can occur when starting exercise, but an individual plan and ongoing support matter.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE NG100 supports specialist physiotherapy and regular exercise suited to the person. Exercise does not replace prescribed treatment for inflammatory arthritis.

Swimming and hydrotherapy are not the same

Swimming usually means moving through the water using swimming strokes. Aquatic exercise can include walking and exercises while standing in water. Hydrotherapy is a planned treatment in water, usually guided by a physiotherapist after an assessment.

The Worcestershire NHS hydrotherapy guide explains that water supports body weight and provides resistance for exercise. Warmth may make muscles and joints feel more comfortable. The amount of support depends on water depth and position, so a single percentage should not be treated as a promise for every activity.

What the research can and cannot tell us

A 2016 Cochrane review found small, short-term improvements in pain, disability and quality of life after aquatic exercise programmes for people with hip or knee osteoarthritis. It assessed exercise programmes, not a particular swimming stroke.

The review compared aquatic exercise with control conditions such as usual care or no aquatic exercise. It does not establish that water exercise is better than land exercise, cures arthritis or repairs cartilage. Results from hip and knee osteoarthritis should not be presented as proof for every type of arthritis.

Before you book a session

  • Ask your physiotherapist or healthcare team whether water exercise suits you, especially after surgery or if you have heart, breathing, balance or other important health problems.
  • Check how you would enter and leave the pool. Ask about steps, rails, a hoist, accessible changing rooms and help that is actually available.
  • Tell the instructor or therapist about your joint problems and any limits in your care plan. Do not assume a general class includes an individual assessment.
  • Ask about depth, water temperature and supervision. Hydrotherapy pools are often warmer than ordinary swimming pools, but hotter is not automatically safer or better for everyone.

The Royal Cornwall NHS hydrotherapy service describes assessment, access and health checks. Its local service is an example, not a promise of the same facilities or eligibility everywhere. Ask your own physiotherapy service about local referral routes and costs before arranging anything.

Finding a comfortable way to move

There is no universally best stroke for an arthritic joint. A stroke that suits one person may aggravate another person's shoulder, neck, hip or knee. A physiotherapist or appropriately qualified instructor can help adapt movement. Water walking or supported exercises may be more suitable than lengths for some people.

Begin with a manageable amount rather than a fixed target from an article. Discuss how to adjust the session if pain, fatigue or other symptoms increase. Do not push through new severe pain. If symptoms remain worse after sessions, ask for your plan to be reviewed rather than automatically increasing time or resistance.

You do not always need to be able to swim for supervised hydrotherapy, but tell the service if you cannot swim or feel anxious. Confirm its depth, support and supervision before entering. A buoyancy aid is not a substitute for suitable supervision.

When not to enter the pool

Contact the service before attending if you feel unwell, have a fever, infection, open wound, recent diarrhoea or vomiting, or a change in your health. Services have different exclusion periods and screening rules. Follow the rules for your own pool and condition rather than using a general waiting time from this article.

New chest pain, unexplained breathlessness or unstable heart or breathing problems need medical assessment, not a trial swim. If you feel faint, dizzy, unwell or develop chest pain during a session, stop and tell staff immediately.

Changing rooms and poolside

  • Allow enough time for changing and resting so you do not have to rush.
  • Ask for help on wet surfaces and use the access equipment agreed with staff.
  • Check that footwear and any walking aid are allowed and suitable for that pool area.
  • Bring what the service asks for and follow its showering and hygiene instructions.

When symptoms need urgent help

Get urgent medical advice for sudden severe joint pain or a newly hot, swollen joint, even without fever. Do not treat this as ordinary post-exercise soreness. In England, Scotland and Wales, contact an urgent GP service or call 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. See NHS septic arthritis advice.

Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, such as gasping or being unable to get words out, or sudden chest pain that does not go away, spreads to the arm, neck or jaw, or comes with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness. Do not drive yourself. See the NHS guides to shortness of breath and chest pain.

Common questions

Is swimming a treatment for every type of arthritis?

No. It is one possible activity. Evidence and suitability depend on the condition and the person. Keep taking prescribed treatment unless your healthcare team advises otherwise.

How long should I swim?

There is no single session length or weekly schedule suitable for everyone. Ask for a plan matched to your symptoms, health and starting ability, then review how you respond.

Can I use NHS hydrotherapy?

Ask your physiotherapist about local services, assessment and referral. Availability and access rules vary. This article does not promise NHS treatment or a particular waiting time.
